To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
calcium-induced exocytosis requires an active G protein.
calcium-induced secretion in RBL cells (i) requires ATP, (ii) requires a vectorially active Ge protein, and (iii) is not mediated by any known second messenger.
calcium-dependent exocytosis in permeabilized RBL cells requires a vectorially active G protein, and this protein is probably not the Gs protein involved in adenylate cyclase activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the calcium-triggered secretory response of permeabilized RBL cells.
the role of G proteins in the regulation of exocytotic release in permeabilized mast cells.
the role of G proteins in calcium-triggered secretion of RBL cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
G proteins are required for exocytosis, but that their role in the process is not yet understood.
G protein-mediated exocytosis, although possible, is still a matter of debate.
a vectorially acting, calcium-dependent Ge protein exists in RBL cells and that it can act in a post-second messenger mode.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
calcium-dependent exocytosis in RBL cells can be triggered by a vectorially acting Ge protein.

the secretory machinery of RBL cells is under the control of at least two different G protein(s), one of which is activated by the second messenger inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, and the other by calcium.
calcium-induced secretion requires ATP, an activated G protein and the correct intracellular pH, whereas the latter two parameters are not sufficient to elicit secretion in the absence of calcium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
calcium-induced exocytosis requires an activated G protein and is inhibited by GTP gamma S, which keeps G proteins in a permanent active conformation.
the calcium-induced exocytotic process in rat basophilic leukemic cells is controlled by an activated G protein.
